chapters.title: Chapter 5: Behavioral Economics in Organizations and the Workplace

lessons.title: Performance Incentives and Motivation Crowding: When Bonuses Backfire

children.text: In 2000, economists Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini studied ten daycare centres in Israel where parents occasionally arrived late to collect their children, an awkward but manageable problem handled through mild social disapproval. The centres introduced a modest fine for pickups more than ten minutes late, expecting the standard economic prediction to hold: raise the cost of a behavior, and you get less of it. Late pickups didn't fall. They roughly doubled, and stayed elevated even after the centres later removed the fine entirely. This lesson is about why adding money to a decision can sometimes destroy exactly the motivation you were counting on.

body.text: Adding an extrinsic incentive to a behavior that already carried an intrinsic or moral motivation can reframe that behavior from "the right thing to do" into "a transaction with a price," and once that reframing happens, removing the incentive afterward does not restore the original motivation. Economists call this motivation crowding, and it explains some of the most counterintuitive failures in incentive design.

children.text: Gneezy and Rustichini titled their paper on the daycare result "A Fine Is a Price," and the title is the finding. Before the fine, arriving late meant breaking a social norm, showing up late imposed a real cost on a teacher waiting around, and most parents felt genuinely bad about it. Once a fine existed, lateness stopped being a moral failing and became a service parents could simply buy: pay a small, known, affordable amount, and the guilt attached to being late disappeared along with it. The fine didn't raise the cost of lateness in any way that mattered to parents who could easily afford it. It removed the actual reason most parents had been arriving on time in the first place.
Motivation Crowding Theory: When Incentives Crowd Out, and When They Crowd In

markDefs.definition: The finding, formalized by economist Bruno Frey, that an external reward or punishment can reduce (crowd out) or increase (crowd in) a person's pre-existing intrinsic motivation for a task, depending on whether the incentive is perceived as controlling or as genuine recognition.

children.text: Economist Bruno Frey formalized this pattern as

, building on psychologist Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's earlier self-determination theory. The key distinction is whether a reward is experienced as controlling, "do this or else," "do this and get paid," or as informational, a genuine signal that someone recognizes your competence or good judgment. Controlling incentives are what tend to crowd out intrinsic motivation, since they shift the felt reason for acting from "I choose to" to "I was made to." Incentives framed as recognition, a bonus explicitly tied to demonstrated skill or genuinely good outcomes rather than raw volume, can instead crowd motivation in, reinforcing rather than replacing someone's sense that they're good at what they do.
Deci's Original Experiment: Where Psychology Found This First

Like bounded rationality in Chapter 1, this idea reached economics from psychology. In 1971, Edward Deci ran an experiment where participants worked on an engaging puzzle task. One group was paid for solving puzzles during part of the session, another group was never paid at all. Deci then gave everyone a free-choice period, with no payment on offer, and simply observed who kept playing with the puzzles for fun. The previously paid group spent noticeably less free-choice time on the puzzles than the never-paid group, despite having found the exact same task genuinely interesting to begin with. Being paid for something you already enjoyed doing seemed to quietly replace "I do this because it's interesting" with "I do this because I get paid," and once the payment stopped, so did much of the enjoyment.

British social researcher Richard Titmuss argued in 1970 that a purely voluntary, unpaid blood donation system could outperform a paid one, because payment turns an act of altruism into a commercial transaction, and some people who would happily donate for free decline to sell something they don't see as a commodity. Decades later, economists Katarina Mellström and Magnus Johannesson ran a controlled test of this claim: offering payment for blood donation. They found women's willingness to donate dropped significantly when payment was introduced, while men's donation rate barely moved, a striking result suggesting the crowding-out effect isn't universal even within the same incentive, and can depend heavily on how differently people relate to the act being incentivized.
When Does This Actually Apply? Three Conditions for Crowding Out

body.text: Motivation crowding is not a universal law that incentives always backfire. It shows up specifically when a task already carried genuine intrinsic or moral motivation, and when the incentive is experienced as controlling rather than as recognition. For tasks with little pre-existing intrinsic content, straightforward mechanical or repetitive work, standard incentives work exactly as classical economics predicts, sometimes dramatically well.

children.text: Economist Edward Lazear's landmark study of Safelite Glass Corporation found exactly this contrast. When the company switched windshield installation technicians from a fixed hourly wage to piece-rate pay, paid per windshield installed, productivity rose by roughly 44%. Installing windshields carries little of the moral or intrinsic content that made the daycare fine backfire. There was no norm being priced out of existence, just a straightforward mechanical task responding to a straightforward incentive exactly as intended.

body.title: Apply the piece-rate effect
body.prompt: Suppose a technician installs 6 windshields a day under a fixed hourly wage. Applying Lazear's finding of roughly a 44% productivity increase under piece-rate pay, approximately how many windshields would that technician install per day under piece-rate pay?
body.explanation: 6 × 1.44 ≈ 8.6 windshields a day. Unlike the daycare fine, this incentive isn't competing against any pre-existing moral motivation to install windshields quickly, so it produces a straightforward, sizeable productivity gain rather than a backfire.

children.text: Indian Workplace Application: Sales Incentives and Mis-Selling Risk

This is precisely the tension Indian financial sector regulators have repeatedly flagged in compensation design. A relationship manager's job carries a genuine intrinsic and professional component, giving a client suitable advice, alongside whatever sales target sits on top of it. A bonus structure paid purely on volume, more policies sold, more loans disbursed, regardless of suitability, risks the exact daycare dynamic: it reframes "recommend what's right for this client" into "sell whatever hits the number," and once that reframing happens, it doesn't reverse just because the target eases up later. This is a meaningful part of why RBI's compensation guidelines for banks, and similar guidance from SEBI and IRDAI, have pushed toward risk-adjusted, deferred, and quality-linked variable pay rather than pure sales-volume bonuses, treating compensation design as a genuine driver of mis-selling risk, not merely a motivation problem.

body.title: Redesigning a cross-selling bonus
body.scenario: A private bank pays relationship managers a bonus purely on the number of insurance and investment products cross-sold each quarter, with no adjustment for whether the product suited the client. Customer complaints about unsuitable product recommendations have risen sharply since the scheme launched.
body.prompt: Using motivation crowding theory, explain what likely went wrong, and propose a redesign.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Relationship managers likely had genuine professional motivation to serve clients well before the scheme existed. A purely volume-based bonus is a controlling incentive that reframes the job from "advise this client well" to "hit this number," the same mechanism behind the daycare fine.
2. Removing the bonus now wouldn't necessarily restore the original service orientation immediately, echoing the daycare finding that the fine's effect persisted even after removal, so the fix needs to be a redesign, not simply a reversal.
3. A better structure would tie variable pay to a blended measure including product suitability, client outcomes, or complaint and reversal rates, alongside volume, shifting the incentive from purely controlling toward something closer to recognition of good client outcomes.
4. Consistent with what RBI-style compensation guidance already encourages, deferring part of the bonus and linking it to sustained client outcomes over volume achieved in a single quarter would reduce the incentive to sell anything just to hit a short-term target.

body.title: Crowding out, or a straightforward incentive?
body.question: A logistics company introduces a piece-rate bonus for warehouse packers, paid per package correctly packed, replacing a fixed hourly wage. Packing speed has no strong pre-existing moral or intrinsic dimension for most packers. What does motivation crowding theory predict here?
options: Crowding out, because any incentive risks backfiring
A straightforward productivity increase, similar to the Safelite Glass piece-rate result, since there's little intrinsic motivation for the incentive to crowd out
No effect at all, since packers were already paid before
Crowding in, because packers will feel their competence is being controlled
body.explanation: Crowding out specifically requires a pre-existing intrinsic or moral motivation for the incentive to displace. Mechanical, repetitive tasks with little such content, like windshield installation or package packing, generally respond to standard incentives in the straightforward direction classical economics predicts.

body.title: Name the effect
body.textWithBlank: When an external reward reduces a person's pre-existing intrinsic motivation for a task, rather than adding to it, economists call this motivation ___.
body.explanation: Motivation crowding out is most likely when a task already carried genuine intrinsic or moral motivation and the incentive is experienced as controlling rather than as recognition of competence.

body.title: Why did the daycare fine's effect outlast the fine itself?

children.text: Gneezy and Rustichini found that removing the fine weeks later did not bring late pickups back down to their original level. Once lateness had been reframed as a purchasable service rather than a breach of a social norm, the original norm didn't simply switch back on when the price disappeared. This is the sharpest warning in motivation crowding research for anyone designing incentives: the damage from a poorly designed controlling incentive can be far more durable than the incentive itself, which is a strong argument for testing compensation changes carefully before rolling them out organization-wide, rather than assuming a bad incentive can simply be reversed later at no cost.

body.label: The daycare fine's effect
body.context: Gneezy and Rustichini's 2000 study found the fine increased, rather than decreased, late pickups, and the effect persisted even after the fine was later removed.

cards.definition: Bruno Frey's finding that external rewards or punishments can crowd out or crowd in a person's pre-existing intrinsic motivation, depending on whether the incentive feels controlling or like genuine recognition.
A reduction in intrinsic motivation caused by introducing an external incentive, most likely when a task already carried moral or intrinsic motivation and the incentive feels controlling.
An increase in motivation caused by an external reward experienced as recognition of competence rather than as control.
Compensation paid per unit of output rather than per hour, shown by Lazear's Safelite Glass study to substantially increase productivity in tasks with little intrinsic motivation to crowd out.

Deci and Ryan's distinction between a reward experienced as "do this or else" versus one experienced as genuine feedback on competence, central to predicting whether an incentive crowds motivation in or out.

points: Motivation crowding theory explains a real, counterintuitive failure mode: adding a fine or bonus to a behavior that already carried intrinsic or moral motivation can reframe it as a mere transaction, reducing the very behavior the incentive was meant to increase.

The daycare fine study's most striking finding wasn't just that lateness increased, it's that removing the fine afterward didn't restore the original motivation, a durable cost worth weighing before rolling out a controlling incentive.

Crowding out is not universal. Tasks with little pre-existing intrinsic content, like piece-rate factory work, generally respond to standard incentives exactly as classical economics predicts, sometimes very strongly.

The deciding factor is usually whether an incentive feels controlling, "do this or get paid," versus informational, genuine recognition of competence, which is why bonus framing matters as much as bonus size.

Indian financial regulators' push toward risk-adjusted, deferred, quality-linked compensation for relationship managers and sales staff is a direct, practical application of motivation crowding theory to a real mis-selling risk, not just an abstract academic finding.
